justification_text:
The point estimates across all horizons—one day (1d), one week (1w), and one month (1m)—are the same at 220.7. This reflects the assumption that the most likely outcome, or the central tendency, of the variable being forecasted does not change significantly over time. That could be because the underlying conditions driving the variable appear stable or because there isn’t a strong reason to believe that the expected value will deviate in any specific direction. Essentially, the point estimates reflect the best guess of where the data will center across each time frame, assuming no major disruptions or shifts in trends.

The widening of the confidence intervals as the forecast horizon extends is driven by increasing uncertainty over time. For example, the 90% confidence interval is narrowest over one day (217.5 to 223.9), wider over one week (213.0 to 228.4), and significantly wider over one month (205.0 to 236.4). This increase reflects the fact that the further away in time we try to predict, the greater the potential for unforeseen variables, randomness, or compounding errors to influence the outcome. Short-term forecasts are less exposed to cumulative variability, so they come with tighter bounds. Over the course of a month, however, there are likely to be more sources of deviation, whether they are small daily fluctuations adding up or unpredictable events.

Specific risks or events could cause outcomes to fall outside these intervals. For instance, if there is an unexpected event or a major shock—such as new policy announcements, geopolitical disruptions, or extreme market volatility—the real outcome might lie beyond the predicted range of the confidence intervals. These intervals are probabilistic, meaning they aim to capture 90% of potential scenarios, but there’s always a 10% chance that outcomes fall above or below the stated bounds. Large deviations might also occur if the assumptions underlying the forecast—that is, smooth trends or stable drivers—fail to hold due to anomalies or unforeseen dynamics in the system being modeled.
